The Tullberg's soft-furred rat, Praomys tullbergi, is a small African murid rodent whose reproductive biology exhibits the rapid pace typical of tropical small mammals. Under standard laboratory conditions maintained at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the duration of gestation averages 24 days [tg = 24 days], a brief intrauterine period that reflects the species’ altricial developmental mode. Parturition yields litters that commonly contain 3.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3.5 pups per litter], a figure consistently recorded across multiple captive breeding colonies. In the wild, this fecundity is likely modulated by seasonal resource availability, though field observations from West African forest remnants suggest comparable litter sizes. When food and thermal conditions remain optimal, females can sustain up to 4 litters per year [F_R_i = 4 litters per year], enabling a remarkably high annual reproductive output. Such a rapid reproductive tempo is characteristic of many Praomys species and contributes to their ecological resilience in fragmented landscapes, where population turnover compensates for elevated predation pressure, a strategy that ensures persistence even in disturbed habitats.

Neonates of Tullberg’s rat are born in an extremely altricial state, with eyes closed and fur absent, weighing only 2.7 grams [Wwb = 2.7 grams] at birth. This birth mass places the species among the smaller-bodied representatives of the genus, yet postnatal growth is rapid when juveniles are reared under the controlled thermal environment of 37 °C [T = 37 °C] that matches the normothermic core temperature of the mother. Nursing continues throughout the early suckling period, and pups remain entirely dependent on maternal milk. The weaning process is completed at 25 days after birth [tx = 25 days after birth], a milestone at which juveniles have reached a wet body mass of 10.5 grams [Wwx = 10.5 grams] at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This nearly fourfold increase in mass over a period of less than four weeks underscores the intense lactational investment and high milk quality provided by the dam. The shift to nutritional independence coincides with the eruption of dentition and the commencement of solid food ingestion, after which growth rates decelerate as juveniles transition into the sub-adult phase.

The asymptotic adult body mass of Praomys tullbergi, attained well after sexual maturity, reaches an ultimate wet weight of 30 grams [Wwi = 30 grams]. This moderate adult size is accompanied by a pronounced sexual dimorphism in the timing of reproductive maturation. Under the same normothermic conditions of 37 °C [T = 37 °C] used throughout captive studies, male rodents typically reach puberty somewhat earlier than their female counterparts. Specifically, the age at which gonadal maturation and the onset of spermatogenesis occur has been documented at 75 days after birth [tp = 75 days after birth] in males at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. In contrast, females exhibit a slightly later pubertal transition, with the first oestrous cycle and attainment of sexual maturity recorded at 82 days after birth [tp = 82 days after birth] at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This differential maturation schedule, in which males become reproductively competent roughly one week before females, is a pattern observed in several rodent species and may reduce the latency of reproduction in wild populations where dispersing males encounter resident females that mature shortly afterward.

Estimates of maximum longevity in Tullberg’s soft-furred rat remain tentative due to the limited duration of most field studies, but captive individuals have survived for approximately 1898 days [am = approximately 1898 days] when maintained at a constant ambient temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This value corresponds to roughly 5.2 years, although the actual figure should be interpreted with caution because sample sizes in laboratory colonies have been modest and senescence-related mortality may be influenced by dietary and housing factors. In wild populations, predation pressure and resource unpredictability likely truncate the lifespan well below this physiological maximum. The available data place this species within the upper range of longevity for small African murids, exceeding the typical 2–3 year maximum observed in many closely related Praomys. The extended lifespan, combined with the rapid reproductive rate documented earlier, suggests that Praomys tullbergi adopts a life-history strategy characterized by high fecundity tempered by moderate iteroparity, a combination that presumably buffers populations against environmental stochasticity.

Beyond these life-history parameters, the ecology of Praomys tullbergi is shaped by its reliance on dense understory vegetation in both primary and secondary forests. The interval between parturition and nutritional independence is relatively brief, spanning just 25 days after birth [tx = 25 days after birth], yet this early independence also exposes juveniles to ectoparasite loads and predation risks at a young age at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. The species is predominantly nocturnal and arboreal, foraging for seeds, fruits, and small arthropods, and its population dynamics are closely tied to seasonal rainfall patterns that influence food availability. Comparative studies across the Praomys genus suggest that P. tullbergi exhibits a body mass at the lower end of the genus range, with adult individuals weighing about 30 g [Wwi = about 30 g] in the wild, a figure consistent with the morphometric data from museum specimens collected throughout West Africa. Its role as a reservoir host for several zoonotic pathogens, including Lassa virus and Leptospira spp., further underscores the importance of understanding its population biology. The combination of small body size, high reproductive capacity, and moderate longevity enables this species to serve as a resilient demographic buffer in the face of habitat disturbance.
